properties.name: Divide
properties.basis: The point is the standing depot, moved from the modern crossroads (OpenStreetMap's village point) 0.42 mile west-south-west, because the depot is the railway place and its position is now established: a Google Maps listing and satellite picture put a single building of depot form here, on the side of US 24 and Highway 67 that drgw.net gives, within about 30 ft. That the building is the depot rests on secondary sources. The junction of the two railways was about 300 ft north-east of it. Elevation is the 1 m lidar ground at the point.
properties.summary: Divide is the town at the top of Ute Pass, where the Colorado Midland Railway crossed its summit on the way west from Colorado Springs and where the Midland Terminal Railway branched off south to the Cripple Creek district. Poor's Manual of 1887 says the Colorado Midland was finished 100 miles west from Colorado Springs by 1 July 1887, which takes in Divide, and Divide is a station in the Colorado Midland's public timetable of October 1888, 27.8 miles from Colorado Springs. The June 1895 timetable names it as the change for the Midland Terminal to Grassy and Cripple Creek, and the Midland Terminal's own tables count their miles from Divide (1895, 1909) and later from Colorado Springs, Divide being mile 26.9 (1920 to 1948, altitude printed 9,198 ft). Secondary sources say the station was first called Hayden's Divide, that the Midland Terminal was begun here in December 1893, that it took over the Colorado Midland's track east of Divide when that railway was given up in 1921 (a Gazette headline of 30 December 1921 reports the purchase), and that the last trains ran in 1949. The post office opened on 26 June 1889 (Wikipedia). The depot still stands south of US 24, about 0.4 mile east of the Highway 67 crossroads and next to the old junction; a 2025 newspaper article says it was built in 1886, burned a year later and was rebuilt in 1903, dates not yet checked against a primary record, and it is being restored. The 1894 and 1901 government maps draw the Colorado Midland climbing to the summit by a loop north of the wagon road, and the 1901 map draws a wye where the Midland Terminal leaves it. On the 1 m lidar the loop survives as a bench now used by Grandview Drive, the summit cut west of the crossroads is about 30 ft deep, and south of the junction the Midland Terminal's bank runs past the reservoir dam east of town and on along the creek. A straight cut beside the loop that the old maps do not show is unexplained. The junction and the wye are built over. The Denver Public Library holds a photograph of the earlier depot of about 1896, and Otto Perry's and Ralph Hallock's photographs of Midland Terminal trains near Divide in 1935 and 1949.
open_questions: The depot's dates: the Gazette (2025) says built 1886, burned a year later, rebuilt 1903; 1904 is also given. 1886 is before the Colorado Midland is said to have reached Divide (1887). Needs a primary record (railway records, a newspaper of 1903 or 1904, the county's designation).
Whether the standing building is on the site of the depot in the c.1896 photograph (DPL X-7727), and where the 1887 depot stood: not established.

Where the junction switch and the wye's legs lay: the 1901 map draws a wye but at 1:125,000; the ground is built over. A faint line south-east of the junction is too steep on today's ground for track and is not taken as a leg.
Water tank, coal, section house, sidings or yard at Divide: no source seen mentions them. The 1901 map shows building symbols near the junction but not what they were.

The straight cut west of the crossroads, south of the loop: OpenStreetMap tags it Colorado Midland, but neither old map shows it and it climbs about 3.4 per cent. A line change after 1901, a siding or a road?
When the loop went out of use, and when the Colorado Midland west of Divide was taken up (1918 stop, 1921 abandonment: the secondary sources differ).

Mileage from Colorado Springs: 27.8 in the Colorado Midland's timetable of October 1888, 26.9 in the Midland Terminal's of 1920 to 1948, 27.4 on drgw.net. The difference may be a line change (the loop given up?) or a different measuring point; not resolved.

Altitude: the Midland Terminal timetables print 9,198 ft for Divide; the 1 m lidar ground is 9,112 ft at the depot and at most about 9,174 ft anywhere on the line inside the box (at the summit cut). Which point the 9,198 refers to is not known.
The depot is not in a timetable as a building; the timetables show only that Divide was a telegraph station from 1893 (a coupon station 1935 to 1940).
The 1894 and 1901 maps draw the loop about 800 ft east of where it lies on the ground; read only shapes from them here.

Photographs: the Denver Public Library and Pikes Peak Library District catalogues were searched by hand on 24 Nov 2026 with about eight keyword combinations (Divide with Midland, depot, station, train, Teller, Midland Terminal). DPL's search does not match phrases and 'Divide' is drowned by the Continental Divide (9,790 hits), so the search is not exhaustive. Where Perry's and Hallock's 'near Divide' views were taken has not been worked out. No image has been fetched.
Newspapers indexed by PPLD and not yet read: Gazette 30 Dec 1921 (Midland Terminal buys the track as far as Divide) and 23 May 1976 (the depot renovated).

Rights: eight of the catalogued photographs are of 1935 and 1949 (Otto Perry) and are marked as library copies that may be shown. That rests on the permission the owner reported, whose terms have not been seen; confirm it covers photographs still in copyright before any is fetched and shown.
properties.notes: The first lidar reading (24 Nov 2026) is now entered as structures: the loop, the summit cut, a straight cut the maps do not show, and the Midland Terminal bank south of the junction. Through the town centre the main line is under US 24 and modern building. Divide is a living town, so most railway ground is built over.

properties.name: Gillett
properties.basis: Platted townsite; position from three registered insurance sheets and 2024 lidar.
properties.summary: A Midland Terminal Railway town in Teller County, Colorado, platted in 1894 on the flats north-east of Cripple Creek. It peaked about 1896 to 1897, held the bullfight of August 1895 in a timber ring inside its racetrack, and faded after 1900. Nothing stands today but the ruin of the Catholic church.
open_questions: Bull ring: position good to about 50 ft; the lens angle of the hill photograph (X-8601) is not settled.
5th Street photograph (X-8657): the standpoint is a guess and the building fronts do not fit the map.
Depot: the street side and the north end are conjecture.
Monte Carlo: orientation good only to about 20 degrees; wall height uncertain.
Catholic church: the north (rear) wall is not shown in any photograph.
Houses placed from the 1897 panorama on the far north-west slope may be 7 to 10 percent too near (evidence from three houses).
122 houses are illustrative placeholders: no photograph in hand gives their positions.
Which dam the 1965 flood photographs show.

local.acknowledgement: This reconstruction began as a response to the photographs of Gillett shared by the Victor Heritage Society. Their photographs are not reproduced here unless their holders have cleared them; each is credited where it is used.

properties.name: Midland
properties.basis: The point is the OpenStreetMap hamlet named Midland. It falls within about 300 ft of the building symbols beside the name Midland on the 1894 and 1901 USGS sheets, so the settlement's position is taken as measured to the accuracy of those maps. The railway grade, plain on the 1 m lidar, passes about 700 ft to the north-east. Where the station itself stood is not established. Elevation is the 3DEP ground at the point.
properties.summary: A small settlement in the valley between Divide and Gillett, and a station on the Midland Terminal Railway. It is in the public timetables from June 1895 (as a Midland Terminal station in the Colorado Midland's table) to March 1948, the last one read, at 6.2 miles from Divide in the tables of 1920 and after. Secondary sources say the first section of the railway was finished to Midland on 9 December 1893. The 1894 government map shows the name and a few buildings beside a road but no railway; the 1901 edition shows the railway passing east of the buildings and then swinging through a wide horseshoe curve to the south-east. The grade is still plain on the ground: a broad bench that bends at Midland and runs off along the hillside. The railway ran until 1949. People still live at Midland. No photograph of the place in railway days has been found yet.
open_questions: Where the station and any siding stood: not established. The 1 m lidar shows a level bench on the inside of the bend in the grade, about 700 ft north-east of the settlement, which would suit a station; that reading is a conjecture until a map, photograph or record confirms it.

No photograph of Midland was found in a first search of the Denver Public Library catalogue on 24 Nov 2026. That search engine does not match phrases, so this is not proof there are none; the Pikes Peak Library District and local museums have not been searched.

How far Midland was from Divide, and when the rails reached it. The timetables give 6.2 miles (1920 to 1948), 6 miles (1909) and 7 miles (June 1895, whole miles from Denver). Wikipedia gives 7.1 miles and 9 December 1893 (citing L. I. Tingvik, 'Rail dates', 2006), and in the same article says the first narrow-gauge track was torn up in January 1893. The date needs a primary source.
'Founded 1893' is given by Wikipedia without a source. Whether Midland had a post office, and when, is not known here.
Elevation: 8,972 ft is the 3DEP ground at the point. The 9,407 ft in the Geographic Names record quoted by Wikipedia belongs to the census area, whose centre is about 0.8 mile to the south-east.
The 1951 and 1994 USGS maps at 1:24,000 have not been cut for Midland: it lies across the edge of two sheets.

Midland is missing from the Midland Terminal's own table of 14 July 1895, which lists only Divide, Gillett, Grassy, Independence and Victor; it appears in the Colorado Midland's table of June 1895. Whether it was then a regular stop is not known.

properties.name: Short Line Tunnel No. 4 (the Granite Tunnel)
properties.basis: Position of the bore from the OpenStreetMap trace of Gold Camp Road, which runs on the railway grade; to be checked against lidar. Identified as Tunnel No. 4 by its length: the trace is about 530 ft, and the Denver Public Library caption gives 521 ft for No. 4, the longest of the nine.
properties.summary: The longest of the nine tunnels on the Colorado Springs and Cripple Creek District Railway, the Short Line, cut through granite without timbering: 521 ft. The line opened in April 1901 and was given up about 1920; its grade became a toll road and then Gold Camp Road. A curved timber trestle led to one portal.
open_questions: The McClure photograph (MCC-83) shows the south portal: its camera solves there to 12 px, and only that portal has a hollow for the trestle. The north portal was not put through the solver, because the ground there has no hollow at all. The camera is good only to about 150 ft.
The tunnel numbering: sources disagree on which tunnels survive and how they are numbered. No. 4 here rests on the length alone.
Dates of the line (opened April 1901, abandoned about 1920 to 1922) are from secondary sources and need a primary one.
The portals read off the lidar are about 440 ft apart, against 521 ft in the library caption and about 530 ft on the map trace; the approach cuts may hide the true portals.

The trestle carried from the photograph to the ground comes out about 500 ft long and up to 70 ft high, but its far end misses the grade by about 45 ft, so its course is good only to about 100 ft. A second photograph, or the trestle footings on the ground, would fix it.
The portal was taken as 16 ft wide and 19 ft from rail to crown to give the photograph its scale. That is an assumption, not a measurement; the bore still exists and could be measured.
